title: Guéraiche, Colonial Systems of Law (French Empire)

slides.title: The système de l'Exclusif and the contradiction the whole text rests on
slides.text: THE RAISON D'ÊTRE OF THE FRENCH COLONIES WAS TO BENEFIT FRANCE. Royal ordinances of the 18th century defined the SYSTÈME DE L'EXCLUSIF, under which the overseas territories were UNDER THE POWER OF METROPOLITAN FRANCE and any trade between France and its colonies was to be FOR THE BENEFIT OF FRANCE. The principles of the Revolution of 1789 and its legacy ran against these provisions of the ancien régime, especially after the consolidation of the republic in the 1880s. IN THEORY FRENCH LAW WAS TO APPLY EQUALLY IN ALL FRENCH TERRITORIES, INCLUDING THOSE OUTSIDE THE METROPOLE — IN PRACTICE IT DID NOT. And here is the sentence on which the whole article rests and which is best memorised verbatim: REPUBLICAN LAW, DEEPLY INFLUENCED BY THE REVOLUTION, WAS MEANT TO BE A MEANS OF EMANCIPATION FOR THE COLONISED POPULATIONS, BUT ON THE GROUND LAW WAS ALSO USED TO COERCE THEM.

terms.def: The order of the 18th-century royal ordinances: overseas territories under the power of the metropole, and all trade for the benefit of France.

cards.q: What is the central contradiction of French colonial law?
cards.a: Republican law, deeply influenced by the Revolution, was meant to be a MEANS OF EMANCIPATION for the colonised populations — but on the ground it was also used to COERCE them. In theory French law was to apply equally in all territories including the overseas ones; in practice it did not.

slides.title: A patchwork of laws and statutes
slides.text: In the colonies a COMBINATION OF DIFFERENT LEGAL INSTRUMENTS was maintained — FORMAL STATUTES, DECREES VOTED OR ISSUED IN PARIS, EXECUTIVE ORDERS AND LOCAL CUSTOMS — and maintained in such a way as to serve the coloniser's interests. After the actual conquest of a territory, LAW WAS TO REPLACE THE POWER OF ARMS, but in almost every case a RIVALRY BETWEEN THE ARMY AND THE CIVIL ADMINISTRATION PERSISTED. The example is ALGERIA: the soldiers, the conquerors of 1830, were reluctant to obey a civil administration whose authority was confirmed by statute only IN DECEMBER 1896 and then in December 1900. In colonies under direct French rule, such as Algeria, the GOVERNOR-GENERAL WAS ALL-POWERFUL. The colonies were governed partly by DECREES OF TWO MINISTRIES in Paris (the interior ministry and the colonial office) and partly by EXECUTIVE ORDERS, which made the representative of the French government the PRINCIPAL SOURCE OF LAW. Most executive and judicial power lay with the governor-general, especially in territories further from France.

cards.q: What was law in the French colonies made of, and where did its real centre of gravity lie?
cards.a: Of formal statutes, decrees voted or issued in Paris, executive orders and local customs. The colonies were governed by the decrees of two ministries (the interior and the colonial office) and by executive orders, which made the government's representative the PRINCIPAL SOURCE OF LAW — most executive and judicial power lay with the GOVERNOR-GENERAL, the more so the further from France.

cards.q: What does the Algerian example show about the relation of army and civil administration?
cards.a: That after conquest law was meant to replace the power of arms, but the rivalry persisted: the soldiers, the conquerors of 1830, were reluctant to obey a civil administration whose authority was confirmed by statute only in December 1896 and then in 1900 — more than sixty years after the conquest.

slides.title: Protectorates and the appearance of autonomy
slides.text: While the French empire was chiefly under DIRECT RULE, PROTECTORATES were also established. To maintain the APPEARANCE OF AUTONOMY, the French left the native rulers a SYMBOLIC LEGISLATIVE POWER and left LOCAL LEGAL INSTITUTIONS UNTOUCHED. After the conquest of MOROCCO IN 1911, for example, the SULTAN was retained as part of the state apparatus: HE SIGNED THE DAHIRS (DECREES) DRAFTED BY HIS VIZIERS — AND APPROVED BY THE FRENCH ADMINISTRATION. In practical terms, however, the country was governed by the French through the RESIDENT-GENERAL. The French moreover tried NOT TO INTERFERE IN CIVIL MATTERS SO LONG AS THEIR AUTHORITY WAS NOT CHALLENGED, and were particularly careful WHERE RELIGION WAS CONCERNED. The courts were usually in the hands of native judges, but ALWAYS UNDER THE CONTROL OF THE FRENCH ADMINISTRATION. And one feature worth knowing: THROUGHOUT THE EMPIRE THE FRENCH WROTE DOWN TRADITIONAL LAW WHERE NO WRITTEN LAW HAD EXISTED BEFORE THEIR ARRIVAL — thus among the BERBER AND KABYLE populations in Algeria and Morocco.

terms.def: A Moroccan decree signed by the sultan — drafted by his viziers and approved by the French administration.

cards.q: How did a French protectorate work, on the example of Morocco?
cards.a: To maintain the appearance of autonomy, the French left the native ruler a symbolic legislative power and left local institutions untouched: after 1911 the sultan signed DAHIRS drafted by his viziers and APPROVED BY THE FRENCH ADMINISTRATION. In fact the resident-general governed.

cards.q: What did the French do where there was no written law?
cards.a: They WROTE DOWN TRADITIONAL LAW — thus among the Berber and Kabyle populations in Algeria and Morocco. Otherwise they did not interfere in civil matters so long as their authority was not challenged, and were especially careful about religion; the courts were run by native judges but always under the administration's control.

slides.title: Law as a means of emancipation
slides.text: Since the Revolution of 1789, French law had been understood as a means of achieving the republican IDEAL OF EQUALITY AMONG MEN, as ART. VI OF THE DECLARATION OF THE RIGHTS OF MAN puts it. But COLONISATION BY ITS VERY NATURE RAN AGAINST THAT PRINCIPLE. In many colonies SLAVERY still existed: after the failed attempt to abolish it under the First Republic in FEBRUARY 1794, it was the abolitionist VICTOR SCHOELCHER (1804–1893) who finally succeeded in PROHIBITING IT IN 1848. The law was proclaimed throughout the empire, but in colonies such as CAMBODIA the local rulers were reluctant to give up so profitable an institution. French officials formally condemned 'INHUMAN' PRACTICES such as bodily mutilation or cannibalism in Equatorial Africa, or death by strangulation in Indochina. With the republic firmly settled at the end of the 19th century, genuine democrats supported the POLICY OF ASSIMILATION, founded on the principle that FRENCH LAW SHOULD APPLY IN ALL FRENCH TERRITORIES AND THAT ALL INHABITANTS OF THE EMPIRE SHOULD BE GRANTED THE SAME RIGHTS AS ANY FRENCH CITIZEN; in the same spirit France unified its customs tariffs in 1892. THIS TENDENCY PREVAILED FROM THE 1870s TO THE MID-1890s.

terms.def: The policy that French law should apply in all territories of the empire and that all its inhabitants should have the same rights as a French citizen. It prevailed from the 1870s to the mid-1890s.

cards.q: What was the policy of assimilation and when did it prevail?
cards.a: The principle that French law should apply in all French territories and that all inhabitants of the empire should be granted THE SAME RIGHTS AS ANY FRENCH CITIZEN. It prevailed from the 1870s to the mid-1890s; in the same spirit France unified its customs tariffs in 1892.

cards.q: When did France abolish slavery, and how did it work out in practice?
cards.a: After a failed attempt under the First Republic in February 1794, it was prohibited in 1848 by Victor Schoelcher. The law was proclaimed throughout the empire, but in colonies such as Cambodia the local rulers were reluctant to give up so profitable an institution.

slides.title: The turn against assimilation and the question of citizenship
slides.text: AFTER THE ESTABLISHMENT OF THE COLONIAL OFFICE IN MARCH 1894 THE OPPONENTS OF ASSIMILATION GAINED GROUND — UNDER THE PRETEXT OF RESPECT FOR LOCAL TRADITIONS. The chief obstacle to equality then remained FRENCH CITIZENSHIP, which was GRANTED TO PEOPLE FROM THE COLONIES ONLY RARELY. And now the sharpest fact of the article: ALTHOUGH ALMOST A MILLION COLONIAL SOLDIERS WERE MOBILISED IN THE FIRST WORLD WAR, TIMID LEGAL REFORMS LEFT THE ACQUISITION OF FULL CITIZENSHIP DIFFICULT. This fed a GROWING RESENTMENT AMONG THE NATIVE ELITE, CONSCIOUS OF ITS INFERIOR POSITION. The POPULAR FRONT OF LÉON BLUM (1872–1950), France's first socialist government (1936–1937), concentrated on domestic questions and devoted little energy to reform in the colonies — yet it did push through the PROHIBITION OF FORCED LABOUR and the establishment of a COLONIAL LABOUR INSPECTORATE.

cards.q: What happened to the policy of assimilation after 1894, and what remained the chief obstacle to equality?
cards.a: After the establishment of the colonial office in March 1894 the opponents of assimilation gained ground UNDER THE PRETEXT OF RESPECT FOR LOCAL TRADITIONS. The chief obstacle remained FRENCH CITIZENSHIP, granted to people from the colonies only rarely — even after almost a million colonial soldiers had been mobilised in the First World War, which fed the resentment of the native elite.

slides.title: Law as a means of coercion: land in Algeria
slides.text: Because the idea of using the colonies for the coloniser's benefit never really disappeared, the 'limitation' of French law on the ground was rarely applied. Settlers were needed, but the French, historically strongly attached to home, rarely went overseas without the prospect of a profitable return — and so STATUTES WERE MADE TO MINIMISE THE SETTLERS' RISK. After the 'PACIFICATION' OF ALGERIA at the end of the 1830s, the administration gave every settler A HOUSE ON A PLOT OF WHICH A THIRD WAS ALREADY UNDER CULTIVATION — the first impulse for the development of the MITIDJA, the most fertile land around Algiers. To satisfy the growing demand for land, THE LOCAL POPULATION WAS SQUEEZED ONTO SMALLER AND LESS PRODUCTIVE PLOTS divided among the tribes. After the defeat by Prussia and the loss of Alsace and Lorraine by the Treaty of Frankfurt in May 1871 came, IN JUNE 1871, A STATUTE ALLOCATING 100,000 HECTARES IN ALGERIA TO NATIVES OF THOSE PROVINCES — land CONFISCATED FROM MOQRANI, chief of the Medjana region, who had rebelled in 1871 in the GREAT KABYLE REVOLT. The policy of confiscations culminated IN JULY 1873 IN A STATUTE THAT FACILITATED THE EXPROPRIATION OF ALGERIANS. In the same spirit FORCED LABOUR was imposed throughout the empire: in theory locals could be compelled to public duties from FIVE DAYS IN INDOCHINA to TWO WEEKS IN EQUATORIAL AFRICA.

cards.q: How did law serve to transfer land in Algeria? Give three steps with dates.
cards.a: After the 'pacification' at the end of the 1830s every settler received a house and a plot of which a third was already cultivated (the development of the Mitidja), and the locals were squeezed onto smaller and poorer plots. IN JUNE 1871 a statute allocated 100,000 hectares to natives of Alsace and Lorraine — land confiscated from Moqrani after the Great Kabyle Revolt. And IN JULY 1873 came a statute facilitating the expropriation of Algerians.

cards.q: How was forced labour regulated in the French empire?
cards.a: It was imposed throughout the empire: in theory locals could be compelled to public duties from FIVE DAYS IN INDOCHINA to TWO WEEKS IN EQUATORIAL AFRICA. It was prohibited only by Léon Blum's Popular Front (1936–1937), which also established a colonial labour inspectorate.

slides.title: The paradox at the end
slides.text: The author's conclusion, and it is a good point of comparison with the British case. FRENCH LAW WAS A MEANS OF JUSTIFYING COLONISATION: the French, like the Americans, were to 'CIVILISE' the native populations, but in reality they MERELY EXPLOITED their colonies. And yet: AFTER INDEPENDENCE MOST COLONIES BENEFITED FROM FRENCH LAW, for example by ADOPTING THE FRENCH CIVIL CODE OF 1804. PARADOXICALLY, FRENCH INFLUENCE WAS MORE PRONOUNCED AFTER INDEPENDENCE. Compare the British case, where Wenzlhuemer says essentially the same: in India the order established by the British remained practically untouched after 1947. The legal legacy of colonialism does not end with colonialism — and in both empires this holds regardless of how different their methods were.

cards.q: What is the paradox of French colonial law according to Guéraiche?
cards.a: That French law served to justify colonisation — the French were to 'civilise' but in fact exploited — and yet most colonies benefited from French law after independence, for example by adopting the Code civil of 1804. FRENCH INFLUENCE WAS MORE PRONOUNCED AFTER INDEPENDENCE.

cards.q: Compare the British and French colonial legal systems in one point they share.
cards.a: The legal legacy survived decolonisation in both: in India the British order remained practically untouched after 1947, and most French colonies adopted the Code civil. The methods differed — British pluralism and codification against French direct rule with protectorates — the outcome did not.
